exercise.text_title: The Volunteer Job I Chose for the Wrong Reason
exercise.article:
I first signed up to volunteer at the community repair workshop because I thought it would look impressive on my CV. I imagined future employers nodding approvingly at my commitment to community service. At the time, I didn’t see it as something particularly meaningful or enjoyable. It was, quite simply, a strategic move.

On my first day, I arrived with a sense of purpose, ready to dive into practical repair tasks. I was eager to prove my worth by fixing broken appliances and gadgets. However, I was surprised when the workshop coordinator asked me to greet visitors and find out what help they needed. This wasn’t what I had in mind. I had envisioned myself as a fixer, not a friendly face at the door.

Despite my initial disappointment, I soon found myself enjoying the role. One particular interaction stands out in my memory. A gentleman came in, visibly embarrassed about not understanding how to fix his toaster. I could see his discomfort, and I realised it was up to me to make him feel at ease. As I explained the repair process, I was careful not to make him feel foolish. To my surprise, I found satisfaction in helping him understand the simple steps involved.

As the weeks went by, I began to take on more responsibilities. I started organising tasks among the volunteers, matching people with different skills to the right projects. I discovered that I enjoyed this coordination role far more than the actual repair work. It was rewarding to see how my efforts helped the workshop run more smoothly.

One day, I made a small mistake while assigning tasks, which led to a bit of confusion. However, this turned into a learning opportunity. I realised that even small errors could teach me valuable lessons about communication and teamwork. This experience only deepened my appreciation for the coordination aspect of the work.

When it came time to update my CV, I realised that the most valuable aspect of my volunteering experience wasn’t the line I could add to my resume. Instead, it was the insight I’d gained into what I truly enjoyed doing. I had always thought that I needed to focus on developing technical skills for a serious career, but this experience taught me otherwise. I found that I was more drawn to roles that involved working with people and organising tasks.

Reflecting on my time at the workshop, I realised that my initial motivation for volunteering had been misguided. The experience had changed my perspective on what I valued in a job. It wasn’t just about the skills I could list on paper, but about finding work that was personally fulfilling. Now, when I look at my CV, I see more than just a list of experiences. I see a journey of self-discovery and a clearer understanding of the kind of work that truly appeals to me.
